sceneHappening: Treasure in clay jars: the light of Christ, and a ministry that does not lose heart
summary: "Therefore seeing we have this ministry, even as we obtained mercy, we don't faint." Paul has renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness or handling God's word deceitfully; by the open statement of the truth he commends himself to every conscience in the sight of God. If the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, "in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, that the light of the Good News of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them." They do not preach themselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and themselves as servants for Jesus' sake. "For it is the God who said, 'Light shall shine out of darkness,' who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." But "we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves." Paul describes being pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, pursued but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed, always carrying in the body the dying of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in their body. "So then death works in us, but life in you." Quoting Psalm 116, "I believed, and therefore I spoke," they believe and speak, knowing that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise them too. Therefore they do not lose heart: though the outward person is decaying, the inward person is being renewed day by day. "For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory, while we don't look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen."
whySettingMatters: The clay jar was the cheapest, most ordinary household container in the ancient world, used for storage and easily broken, and valuables were sometimes hidden inside (the Dead Sea Scrolls were kept in jars). Paul's image is that the treasure of the gospel is carried in fragile, unimpressive people, so that no one mistakes the source of the power. That is a direct answer to opponents in Corinth who impressed people with eloquence and credentials. The list of hardships in 4:8-9 follows a style common in Greek writing, where a wise man's troubles proved his character, but Paul reverses it: his troubles show that the power belongs to God. "The god of this world" (literally "of this age") is usually taken to mean Satan; some commentators read it as a more general power of the present age. The sentence "always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus" is not about masochism but about the way Paul's suffering matches Jesus' and so makes the life of Jesus visible.

people.note: Describes the treasure and the clay jar.
The image of God and the light of the knowledge of God's glory.
The ones for whom Paul's affliction brings life.

questions: "We have this treasure in clay jars." Why does Paul think a fragile messenger is part of the plan?
Paul lists four pairs: pressed but not crushed, perplexed but not despairing, and so on. Which pair speaks most to your own experience?
What does it mean that the "inner person is being renewed day by day" while the outer one is decaying?
"We look not at the things which are seen but at those which are unseen." How does that change how we weigh trouble?
